reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This is a nice study that reports the chemical production and experimental assessment of two new prodrugs of bictegravir with improved pharmacokinetics, as longer half-life and shorter tails. In animal models, NMXBIC provided plasma inhibitory concentrations enough to be administered twice a year. Furthermore, its short PK tail would allow late dose forgiveness, a concern with the currently available ultra-long acting cabotegravir. Given that bictegravir has a good safety profile and greater resistance barrier than cabotegravir, NMXBIC would be more appealing than cabotegravir for both HIV prevention and treatment. Thus, further clinical development of NMXBIC is warranted. The research team has long experience in the development of ultra-long acting drugs and has pioneered several formulations in the HIV and hepatitis fields.
The Discussion is quite simple and would benefit from expanding the scenarios for HIV Treatment and prevention with the adevent of a 6-month potent antiviral such as NMXBIC. Specific comments for the Discussion section:
1. Drug resistance. From the clinical standpoint, two major differences exist between cabotegravir and bictegravir. The first is resistance barrier by HIV. Whereas HIV integrase mutations Q148R and N155H may compromise the activity of cabotegravir, they have not demonstrated to reduce bictegravir efficacy in vivo.
2. Drug interactions. A second difference between cabotegravir and bictegravir refers to its metabolism. Cabotegravir is largely catabolized in the liver by UGT1A1 and in less extent by CYP3A4. Rifampin may induce its metabolism. Overall the potential for drug interactions is lower with bictegravir.
3. Drug volume. The new bictegravir prodrug NMXBIC needs low volume nanosuspensions and may overcome one of the major side effects of current parenteral long-acting cabotegravir formulations, which is local pain at injection sites. They may extent for a few days, with common development of induration and nodules. The data presented by the author’s testing 1 ml injection site reactions of NMXBIC in the New Zealand rabbit model support its favorable safety profile.
4. PK tail. The long PK tail of long-acting cabotegravir accounts for prolonged subtherapeutic drug concentrations when timely dosing is forgotten, favoring development of drug resistance. In contrast, the new bictegravir prodrug NMXBIC depicts a shorter PK tail and may allow dosing forgiveness with lesser risk.
5. Combination options. The opportunity to combine the new bictegravir prodrug NMXBIC with lenacapavir, which is prescribed subcutaneously every 6 months as HIV treatment, opens a further clinical scenario for NMXBIC. Since HIV treatment with long-acting cabotegravir-rilpivirine every 2-months has revolutionized HIV therapeutics, the advent of a new treatment option every 6 months will definitively transform the HIV field and improve patient’s management.
6. Pre-exposure prophylaxis. The new NMXBIC formulation given twice a year should be more appealing than currently approved options, making easier PrEP indication in some developing regions with high HIV endemicity, as in Sub-Saharan Africa, where 25 out of the 40 million HIV-positive persons live.

This manuscript by Nayan et al describes the design, synthesis, and in vitro and in vivo evaluation of novel monomeric and dimeric bictegravir (BIC) ester prodrugs formulated as injectable nanosuspensions. The primary focus is on the dimeric prodrug (NMXBIC), which achieves ultra-long-acting (ULA) antiretroviral drug exposure with a short pharmacokinetic (PK) tail, addressing a key limitation of current long-acting HIV therapies. The study employs comprehensive in vitro and in vivo methods, including pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, efficacy, and safety assessments in rodent and rabbit models. cabotegravir (CAB) and bictegravir (BIC). The first is the barrier to resistance caused by HIV-1 infection.

Response: We agree! CAB has been reported to have a lower genetic barrier to resistance compared
to BIC and DTG [1]. Specific integrase mutations linked to CAB resistance cluster at positions 74,
97, 138, 140, 147, 148, 155, and 263; combinations of these mutations (e.g., Q148H/K/R with G140A/S

[2]. In contrast, BIC retains activity against a broader range of single, double, and triple INSTI mutants

BIC, which affect their susceptibility to drug-drug interactions such as CYP3A4 inducer. Several studies
have shown that BIC is metabolized by cytochrome P450 (CYP)3A and uridine diphosphate-
glucuronosyltransferase UGT1A1. Co-administration of BIC with strong CYP3A and UGT1A1 inducers
such as atazanavir, nilotinib, and rifampicin is contraindicated [5]. Strong UGT1A1 inducers likewise

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors have made substantial improvements to the manuscript. The addition of in vivo efficacy data and the inclusion of statistical analyses throughout the figures and results markedly improve the transparency, rigor, and interpretability of the work. These additions strengthen the manuscript and provide much-needed validation for the claims of antiviral activity and pharmacokinetic performance.
However, several areas where the authors indicate that additional work will be required are not sufficiently caveated or acknowledged in the main text. In particular:
1. Comparative claims — While the rebuttal appropriately explains that head-to-head testing against other long-acting bictegravir formulations was not feasible, the manuscript still contains statements that could be interpreted as implying superiority of the current formulation. These claims should be tempered or explicitly qualified to clarify that no direct comparative studies were performed.
2. Mechanistic interpretation of prodrug release — The manuscript continues to describe prodrug conversion and release as fully efficient, without adequately acknowledging the complexity of in vivo metabolic pathways and the absence of direct data on intermediates or enzyme-specific hydrolysis. The Discussion should explicitly note that while hydrolysis is supported by indirect evidence, a full mechanistic and metabolic characterization remains future work.
3. Stability and CMC development — The authors’ rebuttal mentions that further accelerated stability, sterilization compatibility, and CMC characterization are planned, but these are not discussed in the manuscript. To present a balanced view of translational readiness, the text should acknowledge that such studies are essential future steps to fully derisk the compound for clinical development.
Overall, the manuscript is now much improved in data quality and presentation, but it would benefit from clearer self-containment and transparency in delineating what has been demonstrated versus what remains to be established in future studies.

### Reviewer 1

This is a nice study that reports the chemical production and experimental assessment of two new prodrugs of bictegravir with improved pharmacokinetics, as longer half-life and shorter tails. In animal models, NMXBIC provided plasma inhibitory concentrations enough to be administered twice a year. Furthermore, its short PK tail would allow late dose forgiveness, a concern with the currently available ultra-long acting cabotegravir. Given that bictegravir has a good safety profile and greater resistance barrier than cabotegravir, NMXBIC would be more appealing than cabotegravir for both HIV prevention and treatment. Thus, further clinical development of NMXBIC is warranted. The research team has long experience in the development of ultra-long acting drugs and has pioneered several formulations in the HIV and hepatitis fields.
The Discussion is quite simple and would benefit from expanding the scenarios for HIV Treatment and prevention with the adevent of a 6-month potent antiviral such as NMXBIC. Specific comments for the Discussion section:
1. Drug resistance. From the clinical standpoint, two major differences exist between cabotegravir and bictegravir. The first is resistance barrier by HIV. Whereas HIV integrase mutations Q148R and N155H may compromise the activity of cabotegravir, they have not demonstrated to reduce bictegravir efficacy in vivo.
2. Drug interactions. A second difference between cabotegravir and bictegravir refers to its metabolism. Cabotegravir is largely catabolized in the liver by UGT1A1 and in less extent by CYP3A4. Rifampin may induce its metabolism. Overall the potential for drug interactions is lower with bictegravir.
3. Drug volume. The new bictegravir prodrug NMXBIC needs low volume nanosuspensions and may overcome one of the major side effects of current parenteral long-acting cabotegravir formulations, which is local pain at injection sites. They may extent for a few days, with common development of induration and nodules. The data presented by the author’s testing 1 ml injection site reactions of NMXBIC in the New Zealand rabbit model support its favorable safety profile.
4. PK tail. The long PK tail of long-acting cabotegravir accounts for prolonged subtherapeutic drug concentrations when timely dosing is forgotten, favoring development of drug resistance. In contrast, the new bictegravir prodrug NMXBIC depicts a shorter PK tail and may allow dosing forgiveness with lesser risk.
5. Combination options. The opportunity to combine the new bictegravir prodrug NMXBIC with lenacapavir, which is prescribed subcutaneously every 6 months as HIV treatment, opens a further clinical scenario for NMXBIC. Since HIV treatment with long-acting cabotegravir-rilpivirine every 2-months has revolutionized HIV therapeutics, the advent of a new treatment option every 6 months will definitively transform the HIV field and improve patient’s management.
6. Pre-exposure prophylaxis. The new NMXBIC formulation given twice a year should be more appealing than currently approved options, making easier PrEP indication in some developing regions with high HIV endemicity, as in Sub-Saharan Africa, where 25 out of the 40 million HIV-positive persons live.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript by Nayan et al describes the design, synthesis, and in vitro and in vivo evaluation of novel monomeric and dimeric bictegravir (BIC) ester prodrugs formulated as injectable nanosuspensions. The primary focus is on the dimeric prodrug (NMXBIC), which achieves ultra-long-acting (ULA) antiretroviral drug exposure with a short pharmacokinetic (PK) tail, addressing a key limitation of current long-acting HIV therapies. The study employs comprehensive in vitro and in vivo methods, including pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, efficacy, and safety assessments in rodent and rabbit models. The development of a dimeric BIC prodrug (NMXBIC) with a short PK tail is a significant advancement, potentially overcoming the issue of prolonged subtherapeutic drug exposure seen with existing long-acting injectables. The authors thoroughly characterize the synthesized prodrugs using NMR, FT-IR, mass spectrometry, and XRD, and assess their physicochemical properties, hydrolysis profiles, and antiretroviral activity in vitro.
Notwithstanding the promising data of the prodrugs shown by the authors, a few key experiments are missing to ensure that the conclusions drawn by the authors are valid:
- Statistical tests are completely absent from the manuscript. These need to be conducted, without them any comparative statements should be removed throughout.
- While the manuscript demonstrates sustained BIC plasma levels and in vitro antiviral activity, there is no in vivo efficacy data (e.g., viral load reduction in infected animal models). Such data would strengthen the translational impact and provide direct evidence of therapeutic benefit
- The manuscript references other long-acting BIC formulations but does not provide direct head-to-head experimental comparisons in their models. Including such data is necessary to contextualize the advantages of the here developed prodrugs more clearly.
- While the study infers hydrolysis mechanisms from plasma/tissue BIC levels, this is insufficient evidence for the metabolic fate and prodrug release. Identification of hydrolysis intermediates (e.g., monomeric BIC-lipid conjugates for MXBIC) should be conducted. Enzyme-specific hydrolysis assays (e.g., carboxylesterase knockdown models) would further delineate esterase specificity of prodrug release and indicate tissue selectivity of the prodrugs. Biliary/fecal excretion profiles should be conducted in vivo to rule out intact prodrug elimination and therefore incomplete prodrug conversion in vivo.
- While prodrug stability was assessed room temperature, it should be investigated at accelerated conditions (e.g., 50°C/75% RH) to further delineate stability. It would also be important to assess stability under clinical-grade sterilization (e.g., autoclaving, filtration) to assess the clinical translatability of the developed prodrugs and formulations.
- While injection site reactions were minimal to moderate in rabbits, the long-term implications of repeated dosing, especially in humans, warrant further discussion in the manuscript.
Minor comments:
- The brackets indicating the extended tail seem to be missing in Figure 1B for MXBIC.
- Error bars should be shown as SD instead of SEM in several of the line plots to more clearly indicate experimental variability, e.g. Fig 1E, 1F, 2A, 2B, 3A, 3B, 4A, 4B, 5A, 5B.
- Standard deviations of PK parameters should be indicated in the Tables in Fig 4C and 5C.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

This is a nice study that reports the chemical production and experimental assessment of two new prodrugs of bictegravir with improved pharmacokinetics, as longer half-life and shorter tails. In animal models, NMXBIC provided plasma inhibitory concentrations enough to be administered twice a year. Furthermore, its short PK tail would allow late dose forgiveness, a concern with the currently available ultra-long acting cabotegravir. Given that bictegravir has a good safety profile and greater resistance barrier than cabotegravir, NMXBIC would be more appealing than cabotegravir for both HIV prevention and treatment. Thus, further clinical development of NMXBIC is warranted. The research team has long experience in the development of ultra-long acting drugs and has pioneered several formulations in the HIV and hepatitis fields.
The Discussion is quite simple and would benefit from expanding the scenarios for HIV Treatment and prevention with the adevent of a 6-month potent antiviral such as NMXBIC. Specific comments for the Discussion section:
1. Drug resistance. From the clinical standpoint, two major differences exist between cabotegravir and bictegravir. The first is resistance barrier by HIV. Whereas HIV integrase mutations Q148R and N155H may compromise the activity of cabotegravir, they have not demonstrated to reduce bictegravir efficacy in vivo.
2. Drug interactions. A second difference between cabotegravir and bictegravir refers to its metabolism. Cabotegravir is largely catabolized in the liver by UGT1A1 and in less extent by CYP3A4. Rifampin may induce its metabolism. Overall the potential for drug interactions is lower with bictegravir.
3. Drug volume. The new bictegravir prodrug NMXBIC needs low volume nanosuspensions and may overcome one of the major side effects of current parenteral long-acting cabotegravir formulations, which is local pain at injection sites. They may extent for a few days, with common development of induration and nodules. The data presented by the author’s testing 1 ml injection site reactions of NMXBIC in the New Zealand rabbit model support its favorable safety profile.
4. PK tail. The long PK tail of long-acting cabotegravir accounts for prolonged subtherapeutic drug concentrations when timely dosing is forgotten, favoring development of drug resistance. In contrast, the new bictegravir prodrug NMXBIC depicts a shorter PK tail and may allow dosing forgiveness with lesser risk.
5. Combination options. The opportunity to combine the new bictegravir prodrug NMXBIC with lenacapavir, which is prescribed subcutaneously every 6 months as HIV treatment, opens a further clinical scenario for NMXBIC. Since HIV treatment with long-acting cabotegravir-rilpivirine every 2-months has revolutionized HIV therapeutics, the advent of a new treatment option every 6 months will definitively transform the HIV field and improve patient’s management.
6. Pre-exposure prophylaxis. The new NMXBIC formulation given twice a year should be more appealing than currently approved options, making easier PrEP indication in some developing regions with high HIV endemicity, as in Sub-Saharan Africa, where 25 out of the 40 million HIV-positive persons live.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript by Nayan et al describes the design, synthesis, and in vitro and in vivo evaluation of novel monomeric and dimeric bictegravir (BIC) ester prodrugs formulated as injectable nanosuspensions. The primary focus is on the dimeric prodrug (NMXBIC), which achieves ultra-long-acting (ULA) antiretroviral drug exposure with a short pharmacokinetic (PK) tail, addressing a key limitation of current long-acting HIV therapies. The study employs comprehensive in vitro and in vivo methods, including pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, efficacy, and safety assessments in rodent and rabbit models. The development of a dimeric BIC prodrug (NMXBIC) with a short PK tail is a significant advancement, potentially overcoming the issue of prolonged subtherapeutic drug exposure seen with existing long-acting injectables. The authors thoroughly characterize the synthesized prodrugs using NMR, FT-IR, mass spectrometry, and XRD, and assess their physicochemical properties, hydrolysis profiles, and antiretroviral activity in vitro.
Notwithstanding the promising data of the prodrugs shown by the authors, a few key experiments are missing to ensure that the conclusions drawn by the authors are valid:
- Statistical tests are completely absent from the manuscript. These need to be conducted, without them any comparative statements should be removed throughout.
- While the manuscript demonstrates sustained BIC plasma levels and in vitro antiviral activity, there is no in vivo efficacy data (e.g., viral load reduction in infected animal models). Such data would strengthen the translational impact and provide direct evidence of therapeutic benefit
- The manuscript references other long-acting BIC formulations but does not provide direct head-to-head experimental comparisons in their models. Including such data is necessary to contextualize the advantages of the here developed prodrugs more clearly.
- While the study infers hydrolysis mechanisms from plasma/tissue BIC levels, this is insufficient evidence for the metabolic fate and prodrug release. Identification of hydrolysis intermediates (e.g., monomeric BIC-lipid conjugates for MXBIC) should be conducted. Enzyme-specific hydrolysis assays (e.g., carboxylesterase knockdown models) would further delineate esterase specificity of prodrug release and indicate tissue selectivity of the prodrugs. Biliary/fecal excretion profiles should be conducted in vivo to rule out intact prodrug elimination and therefore incomplete prodrug conversion in vivo.

### Reviewer 2

The authors have made substantial improvements to the manuscript. The addition of in vivo efficacy data and the inclusion of statistical analyses throughout the figures and results markedly improve the transparency, rigor, and interpretability of the work. These additions strengthen the manuscript and provide much-needed validation for the claims of antiviral activity and pharmacokinetic performance.
However, several areas where the authors indicate that additional work will be required are not sufficiently caveated or acknowledged in the main text. In particular:
1. Comparative claims — While the rebuttal appropriately explains that head-to-head testing against other long-acting bictegravir formulations was not feasible, the manuscript still contains statements that could be interpreted as implying superiority of the current formulation. These claims should be tempered or explicitly qualified to clarify that no direct comparative studies were performed.
2. Mechanistic interpretation of prodrug release — The manuscript continues to describe prodrug conversion and release as fully efficient, without adequately acknowledging the complexity of in vivo metabolic pathways and the absence of direct data on intermediates or enzyme-specific hydrolysis. The Discussion should explicitly note that while hydrolysis is supported by indirect evidence, a full mechanistic and metabolic characterization remains future work.
3. Stability and CMC development — The authors’ rebuttal mentions that further accelerated stability, sterilization compatibility, and CMC characterization are planned, but these are not discussed in the manuscript. To present a balanced view of translational readiness, the text should acknowledge that such studies are essential future steps to fully derisk the compound for clinical development.
Overall, the manuscript is now much improved in data quality and presentation, but it would benefit from clearer self-containment and transparency in delineating what has been demonstrated versus what remains to be established in future studies.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

This is a nice study that reports the chemical production and experimental assessment of two new prodrugs of bictegravir with improved pharmacokinetics, as longer half-life and shorter tails. In animal models, NMXBIC provided plasma inhibitory concentrations enough to be administered twice a year. Furthermore, its short PK tail would allow late dose forgiveness, a concern with the currently available ultra-long acting cabotegravir. Given that bictegravir has a good safety profile and greater resistance barrier than cabotegravir, NMXBIC would be more appealing than cabotegravir for both HIV prevention and treatment. Thus, further clinical development of NMXBIC is warranted. The research team has long experience in the development of ultra-long acting drugs and has pioneered several formulations in the HIV and hepatitis fields.
The Discussion is quite simple and would benefit from expanding the scenarios for HIV Treatment and prevention with the adevent of a 6-month potent antiviral such as NMXBIC. Specific comments for the Discussion section:
1. Drug resistance. From the clinical standpoint, two major differences exist between cabotegravir and bictegravir. The first is resistance barrier by HIV. Whereas HIV integrase mutations Q148R and N155H may compromise the activity of cabotegravir, they have not demonstrated to reduce bictegravir efficacy in vivo.
2. Drug interactions. A second difference between cabotegravir and bictegravir refers to its metabolism. Cabotegravir is largely catabolized in the liver by UGT1A1 and in less extent by CYP3A4. Rifampin may induce its metabolism. Overall the potential for drug interactions is lower with bictegravir.
3. Drug volume. The new bictegravir prodrug NMXBIC needs low volume nanosuspensions and may overcome one of the major side effects of current parenteral long-acting cabotegravir formulations, which is local pain at injection sites. They may extent for a few days, with common development of induration and nodules. The data presented by the author’s testing 1 ml injection site reactions of NMXBIC in the New Zealand rabbit model support its favorable safety profile.
4. PK tail. The long PK tail of long-acting cabotegravir accounts for prolonged subtherapeutic drug concentrations when timely dosing is forgotten, favoring development of drug resistance. In contrast, the new bictegravir prodrug NMXBIC depicts a shorter PK tail and may allow dosing forgiveness with lesser risk.
5. Combination options. The opportunity to combine the new bictegravir prodrug NMXBIC with lenacapavir, which is prescribed subcutaneously every 6 months as HIV treatment, opens a further clinical scenario for NMXBIC. Since HIV treatment with long-acting cabotegravir-rilpivirine every 2-months has revolutionized HIV therapeutics, the advent of a new treatment option every 6 months will definitively transform the HIV field and improve patient’s management.
6. Pre-exposure prophylaxis. The new NMXBIC formulation given twice a year should be more appealing than currently approved options, making easier PrEP indication in some developing regions with high HIV endemicity, as in Sub-Saharan Africa, where 25 out of the 40 million HIV-positive persons live.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript by Nayan et al describes the design, synthesis, and in vitro and in vivo evaluation of novel monomeric and dimeric bictegravir (BIC) ester prodrugs formulated as injectable nanosuspensions. The primary focus is on the dimeric prodrug (NMXBIC), which achieves ultra-long-acting (ULA) antiretroviral drug exposure with a short pharmacokinetic (PK) tail, addressing a key limitation of current long-acting HIV therapies. The study employs comprehensive in vitro and in vivo methods, including pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, efficacy, and safety assessments in rodent and rabbit models. The development of a dimeric BIC prodrug (NMXBIC) with a short PK tail is a significant advancement, potentially overcoming the issue of prolonged subtherapeutic drug exposure seen with existing long-acting injectables. The authors thoroughly characterize the synthesized prodrugs using NMR, FT-IR, mass spectrometry, and XRD, and assess their physicochemical properties, hydrolysis profiles, and antiretroviral activity in vitro.
Notwithstanding the promising data of the prodrugs shown by the authors, a few key experiments are missing to ensure that the conclusions drawn by the authors are valid:
- Statistical tests are completely absent from the manuscript. These need to be conducted, without them any comparative statements should be removed throughout.
- While the manuscript demonstrates sustained BIC plasma levels and in vitro antiviral activity, there is no in vivo efficacy data (e.g., viral load reduction in infected animal models). Such data would strengthen the translational impact and provide direct evidence of therapeutic benefit
- The manuscript references other long-acting BIC formulations but does not provide direct head-to-head experimental comparisons in their models. Including such data is necessary to contextualize the advantages of the here developed prodrugs more clearly.
- While the study infers hydrolysis mechanisms from plasma/tissue BIC levels, this is insufficient evidence for the metabolic fate and prodrug release. Identification of hydrolysis intermediates (e.g., monomeric BIC-lipid conjugates for MXBIC) should be conducted. Enzyme-specific hydrolysis assays (e.g., carboxylesterase knockdown models) would further delineate esterase specificity of prodrug release and indicate tissue selectivity of the prodrugs. Biliary/fecal excretion profiles should be conducted in vivo to rule out intact prodrug elimination and therefore incomplete prodrug conversion in vivo.
- While prodrug stability was assessed room temperature, it should be investigated at accelerated conditions (e.g., 50°C/75% RH) to further delineate stability. It would also be important to assess stability under clinical-grade sterilization (e.g., autoclaving, filtration) to assess the clinical translatability of the developed prodrugs and formulations.
- While injection site reactions were minimal to moderate in rabbits, the long-term implications of repeated dosing, especially in humans, warrant further discussion in the manuscript.
Minor comments:
- The brackets indicating the extended tail seem to be missing in Figure 1B for MXBIC.
- Error bars should be shown as SD instead of SEM in several of the line plots to more clearly indicate experimental variability, e.g. Fig 1E, 1F, 2A, 2B, 3A, 3B, 4A, 4B, 5A, 5B.
- Standard deviations of PK parameters should be indicated in the Tables in Fig 4C and 5C.

antiretroviral activities were assessed in vitro. Notwithstanding the promising data of the prodrugs shown
by the authors, a few key experiments are missing to ensure that the conclusions drawn by the authors
are valid:”
Response: Understood and appreciated. As suggested, these comments have been addressed in detail.
The missing few experiments were focused on data analysis and interpretations, and each were corrected

Point 3. “While the manuscript demonstrates sustained BIC plasma levels and in vitro antiviral activity,
there is no in vivo efficacy data (e.g., viral load reduction in infected animal models). Such data would
strengthen the translational impact and provide direct evidence of therapeutic benefit”
Response: We agree and have added new data demonstrating efficacy of bictegravir monotherapy in a
mouse model of HIV infection. Proof-of-concept viral restriction study in hu-PBL mice demonstrated that
single IM doses of 50, 100, and 200 mg BIC. eq./kg of MXBIC monotherapy sustain suppression of
plasma viral load. This is remarkable compared to our prior observations with cabotegravir injectable in
this mouse model (Biomaterials 151, 53-65 (2018). (Please refer to lines 314-320 and 417-425 of the
main text. Supplementary Figure 24 demonstrates proof of concept efficacy data in NSG PBL humanized
mice)
Point 4. “The manuscript references other long-acting BIC formulations but does not provide direct head-
to-head experimental comparisons in their models. Including such data is necessary to contextualize the
advantages of the here developed prodrugs more clearly.”
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important suggestion. However, direct head-to-head
comparison of proprietary drug delivery technologies described by others in our models is not feasible.
NMXBIC and NM2BIC formulations are highly differentiated from those referenced. Our injectable
prodrug formulations are aqueous nanosuspensions of chemically distinct compounds (prodrugs) versus
device or polymeric based nanoparticles loaded with native bictegravir. We also note that other
differences are linked to (i) primary depot compartments for each technology (intradermal vs.
intramuscular), (ii) drug release mechanisms (polymer erosion/diffusion vs. particle and prodrug
dissolution/hydrolysis), and (iii) lymphatic trafficking. However, we reiterate that animal studies to date
support significantly longer half-life and dosing interval, attenuated peak-to-trough pharmacokinetics, and
well tolerated injections for our aqueous based bictegravir prodrug formulations versus those described
in the literature (lines 402-405 of the main text were rewritten with appropriate references to clarify prior
alternative long-acting BIC approaches).
Point 5. “While the study infers hydrolysis mechanisms from plasma/tissue BIC levels, this is insufficient
evidence for the metabolic fate and prodrug release. Identification of hydrolysis intermediates (e.g.,
monomeric BIC-lipid conjugates for MXBIC) should be conducted. Enzyme-specific hydrolysis assays
(e.g., carboxylesterase knockdown models) can further delineate the esterase specificity of prodrug
release and indicate the tissue selectivity of the prodrugs. Biliary/fecal excretion profiles should be
conducted in vivo to rule out intact prodrug elimination and therefore incomplete prodrug conversion in
vivo.”
Response: We agree that metabolic studies of new chemical entities is scientifically warranted and
required; however, radiochemical synthesis of the lipids and prodrugs, and multi-matrix bioanalytical
method development required for these studies is beyond the scope and goal of our preclinical study.
There are no FDA approved long acting bictegravir formulations and our study sought to identify an ultra-
long acting injectable bictegravir prodrug formulation with a short PK tail. Our prodrugs are transient and
are efficiently hydrolyzed into bictegravir upon dissolution from the particle. Extensive hydrolysis studies
on similar prodrug nanocrystals from our laboratory have demonstrated equal involvement of both
enzymatic and chemical hydrolysis in our ultra-long-acting prodrug activation to release parent drugs with
known metabolic pathway and biocompatible linkages [8-10]. Identification of intermediates, esterase
mapping, will be addressed in follow-up studies with clinical grade compounds and formulations (please
refer to lines 121-122, 443-444 and 447-450 of the main text).
Point 6. “While prodrug stability was assessed room temperature, it should be investigated at accelerated
conditions (e.g., 50°C/75% RH) to further delineate stability. It would also be important to assess stability
under clinical-grade sterilization (e.g., autoclaving, filtration) to assess the clinical translatability of the
developed prodrugs and formulations.”
Response: We appreciate this comment and agree that stability under accelerated conditions and
compatibility with clinical-grade sterilization are essential elements of a future CMC program. Our present
work, however, is a preclinical study focused on prodrug screening and identification of novel ultralong
acting BIC formulations for future clinical development. NM2BIC and NMXBIC have been licensed TO
Exavir Therapeutics Inc. for clinical development. It is also worth noting that our aqueous prodrug
nanosuspensions are compatible with terminal sterilization by gamma irradiation. This was demonstrated
for another licensed program from our laboratory that is undergoing clinical development.
